repetition.avoid: Item: the ending, from cue to-desk to cue last-chord (the vamp, lines your-best to work-with, and the block lift). Kind: segment shape, with its staging. What it repeats: the show has already finished a song by dropping the lights, stopping the music to single out the host in a short spoken exchange, and then bringing the whole band back on the hook with a word changed so that he is taken into the song. The opening, the verses, the hook and the genre may stay as they are. A turn: open.
repetition.why: Fresh in most of what the brief asks about, and a repeat in the one place the writer pointed at. GENRE: fresh. Doo-wop (swung, brushes, a bass on two syllables, no kick, claps or shouts) will not be heard as the aired stomp-clap anthem. STRUCTURAL JOKE: fresh. Here the week's phrase ends on the genre's own syllable, the filler is the whole hook and the key moves to meet a wrong note; the aired song's joke was a spoken line answering every sung wish in a stop bar. MESSAGE, through the opening, the verses and the first two hooks: fresh. It is about what is offered, not about wanting somewhere to be. THE HOOK WITH A WORD CHANGED: fresh taken alone. The bible's bones ask every song for it, and here the word changes who is addressed, not whether a want is met. Whichever of the two songs airs, it will be two aired songs of two that finish on a hook with one word changed, and the next one should be judged as a signature. THE ENDING: repeat. Aired (001, song, from the breakdown to the button): lights down to a spotlight with the host alone and near sincere; a stop in which another character tells him flatly that he is inside the song, with a pin on him to say so; lights up and everyone on the chorus with its words changed to include him; then the host alone for a tag; then a band member's line. Here (from cue to-desk to the tag): the bulbs dim to one spot on the desk; a stop in which the host says he only hosts, gives one note, and Hy takes it flatly, with a tag naming the new key as his; every bulb on and everyone on the hook with one word changed, sung to him and then to the lens, his note the bottom of the chord; then the host alone for the button; then two band members' tag. One sentence covers both without naming a subject: the lights drop, the music stops, the host is singled out and told in a flat line that he is in, and the full band comes back on the hook with a word changed to take him in. That is the recorded device (lights down and a spotlight for a near-sincere breakdown, then the punch) doing the same job at the same point of the same format; it is the same order of moves from the turn to the last line; and it is the feeling the record logs as the aired episode's sincere kind, belonging. The writer was steered off wanting a place and arrived at being given one: the script's own header says the key becomes the host's 'home note'. It is not a turn, because the expectation the aired song left (when the song stops for the host, he is taken in) is met here, not defeated. A turn is open: I find no turned item in the present cut. NOT BLOCKS, for the project manager. (1) Half the verse goes back over things this episode has already shown (the cat voice; the coffee simulator, with that segment's own sketch as its tile), each drawn as a tile as it is sung. That is the aired song's recap of the night's builds in a half dose and without its stamps. Verses that name the window's specifics with a picture each are what the format asks for, so I do not block it and would not block it in a redraft; where the song sits decides how much it plays as a recap. (2) 'built' is sung twice as the plain verb of a list and never ends a sentence; fitting must not change that. (3) The mug landing in the simulator's tile on its sung word, with an ADDED BY tag and an aww, is near the aired staging of a thing arriving on its word. Nobody asks for it and no time is given, so it passes; it should stay a credit and get no flourish. (4) The aired host sang lead through a whole song, so a returning viewer knows he has more than one note; nothing leans on that, and it costs the bridge a little truth. (5) In the present order the song is again second from last, as it was in the aired episode.

message: It leaves a viewer with the thought that the little you have is worth handing over, because around here somebody will work with it: a whole simulator went up under a four-word shrug, a photo of a mug ended up inside it, and a band with two syllables made a song out of them. The hook and the mug couplet are this week's and no other's (the phrase is one member's own words from Tuesday, and the pun exists only because of them), so the song does what the owner asked and wears it lightly, with no line saying it; what could be sung any week is the last twenty seconds, where the feeling lands on the host and not on anything the week did.
airWhy: As the two stand today, the present song: the alternative is the better song on every row and carries the message the owner asked for, but its last twenty seconds are an ending the show has already aired, and I would air it in place of the present song only once that ending is its own.
inside: Straight after the coffee segment it is a repeat, not a callback: Larry lands 'The best we can do.' as a button, and within seconds the same post card is back and he reads the same four words again as a setup, after which the phrase or a variant is said, sung or shown about nine more times in seventy seconds, so the coffee segment's button becomes the song's first line and stops being a punch; with a segment or more between them the same pick-up is a true callback, and the song's own opening already supplies everything it needs. Four members in two segments each is not by itself too hard a lean (one glance-sized tile each, nobody voiced, nobody named in the lyric, and for cee and Samantha the tile is for a different thing from the one the episode showed), but the song then brings no new person to the episode, Dave's one post is performed twice about two minutes apart, and the one to weigh is Samantha, who spoke in the last aired episode and is already the named maker of the opening segment, though the mug can only be hers. Two more things a viewer would meet in this order: the coffee segment has just ended on another member's mug being filled, so 'that mug' will be taken for the wrong one; and 'I only host.' with 'I do what I can.' would make the song the third segment of the night to end on Larry making himself small, after the account bit and the making-of, and the second to turn to the viewer about what they bring.
